title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to test whether interposing a deterministic network verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated device configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical initial LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 72 complete pairs (planned model_calls_used = 72, completed_episode_count = 144). Primary result: every baseline generation produced a valid, non‑faulting emulator execution (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected‑fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Confirmatory interpretation: for the chosen model, task set, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the verifier did not reduce undetected faults because none occurred in the baseline (a ceiling effect). We report preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, exact analysis outputs, representative validator traces, and concrete limitations; and we emphasise that alternate designs (adversarial/fault‑injection testsets, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model sampling) are required to evaluate verifier utility under non‑degenerate error regimes.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) promise to translate operator intent into device‑level network configurations, potentially reducing manual effort in NetOps. Prior work documents encouraging intent→configuration translation accuracy on curated examples but warns of operational risks from semantic errors, incorrect ordering, and protocol misuse that can produce policy violations or outages [1], [2]. A canonical mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that places deterministic validators (header‑space/policy checkers) between generation and execution to detect violations before changes are applied [3]. Despite proposed architectures and prototype systems, there is limited publicly available, end‑to‑end experimental evidence quantifying how much a verifier reduces executed, undetected faults on realistic tasks. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 to answer: Does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the proportion of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults compared to executing the same candidate without verification? Crucially, our confirmatory design uses shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial generation is produced per intent and that identical candidate is evaluated under both baseline (execute) and guarded (verify‑then‑execute-if-not‑flagged) conditions. This isolates verifier detection performance on identical outputs rather than conflating generation differences.
sections.related_work: LLM‑driven intent→configuration translation has been demonstrated in constrained settings and vendor dialects with promising task accuracy [1]. Prototypes and system reports integrate validators and multi‑agent tool orchestration to reduce regressions in NetOps workflows [2]. Generate–verify–repair patterns have been formalised and empirically used in code repair and regulated engineering domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checks [3]. Constraint‑enforcing decoding and retrieval grounding reduce constraint violations in structured outputs in other domains [4]. Classical network verifiers (header‑space, NetPlumber, Batfish) provide fast reachability and policy checks and are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [5]. However, direct, preregistered empirical studies coupling LLMs with canonical network verifiers and measuring emulator execution outcomes are scarce; our work fills this methodological evidence gap by executing a deterministic, paired test and publishing deterministic artifacts and analysis.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational faults: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory hypotheses (H1/H2), exploratory questions, sampling, exclusion, multiplicity, and analysis procedures were frozen before observing outcomes and archived (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the manifest). Design and sampling: a confirmatory paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics; planned N=72 paired intents stratified evenly across three topology complexity strata. Generation: all initial generations used the declared_model_version gpt-5-mini. The recorded execution model configuration shows sampling fields unset (execution/model_configuration.json: temperature = null); null indicates no explicit sampling parameter was specified in the run artifact and provider defaults were used (this residual uncertainty is archived). Adapter and verifier: the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter produced one shared initial generation per intent; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed syntactic and semantic intent‑constraint checks, computed a validation_before/after trace, flagged violations, and followed the preregistered rule: flagged verifier violations render the guarded outcome as "prevented" (no undetected executed fault) without executing the candidate in the emulator. Task generation and constraints: tasks were drawn from a deterministic, documented task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); each task includes an explicit intent, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and expected_final_state recorded in task_manifest entries. Contamination and exclusion rules: exact‑match provenance checks against public corpora were applied; exact matches are flagged and excluded from confirmatory analysis per preregistration. Missingness, retries and technical failures: one initial generation call per task (allowed transient retries as specified); preregistered missingness sensitivity analyses treat excluded pairs conservatively as failures. Analysis procedures: paired_binary_analysis_v1 executed the primary paired binary inference (exact McNemar two‑sided test where applicable) and bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples; seed 1729) for descriptive rates. All analysis code and data artifacts (raw_results.jsonl, paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv) are archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the registered run completed successfully. Planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72 (one shared initial generation per pair, recorded in provider_call_audit). All 72 preregistered confirmatory pairs completed and were scorable; no pairs were excluded. Scoring and validator behaviour: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation rules to the shared candidate and produced validator traces (validation_before/validation_after) for every episode; the scorer_id and version are present in scoring artifacts and show score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION for the sampled examples. Primary contingency and inferential results: the paired contingency table aggregated across 72 pairs is n_11 = 72 (both baseline and guarded succeeded without emulator faults), n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. The estimated paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Interpretation of statistical outputs: the CI is degenerate because there was no observed variation across pairs; the exact test reports no evidence of a difference because the baseline already had zero executed faults. Secondary estimands: verifier detection rates (true positive/false negative) cannot be estimated here because baseline executed faults were absent; no verifier flags led to emulator‑observed faults. Representative artifacts: we present multiple task‑level scoring traces in the archived evidence bundle (execution/scoring/task-00000{1..6}-*.json) where the shared_initial_candidate, validator_trace (validation_before/after), normalized_configuration, and final_state are documented; these artifacts show validator_version = "5.0", parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and difficulty strata metadata. Provider audit: deterministic_reconciliation and provider_call_audit report hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 72, and single stage shared_initial_generation = 72.
sections.discussion: Confirmatory interpretation and ceiling effect: the preregistered paired design required baseline executed faults for a verifier to reduce the undetected‑fault proportion. Observing zero baseline faults produces a valid, evidence‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome: H1 (a paired reduction) is not supported because there were no undetected faults to reduce. This result is meaningful: it documents that, for this specific LLM (gpt-5-mini configured under provider defaults), task bank, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, generator outputs were uniformly valid on our emulated tasks and verifier interposition produced no additional prevention. Design implications for GVR evaluation: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics precisely measure whether a verifier detects faults in the same candidate, but they cannot measure verifier value that arises via triggering repairs or alternative generations unless repair calls are explicitly used; (2) independent per‑condition generation arms or multi‑sample generation (multiple stochastic draws per task) would increase the chance of generator errors and therefore the statistical power to detect verifier benefits; (3) adversarial or fault‑injection task sets intentionally increase generator error prevalence and better test verifier detection performance. Threats to validity: single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) limits external generalisability; synthetic/emulated tasks differ from production devices and live traffic; sampling parameters were unset in the recorded configuration (temperature = null) and provider default sampling semantics are a residual uncertainty (archived in model_configuration.json). Operational implications: absence of baseline faults in a controlled corpus suggests that model+prompt choices and constrained vendor dialects can produce high task accuracy in curated settings, but it does not imply safe production execution generally—robust verification and broader stress testing remain necessary. Reproducibility and artifacts: all raw_results, scoring traces, model_configuration.json, execution manifest, paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, and deterministic_reconciliation.json are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle; representative task and response artifacts are referenced in the paper to enable deterministic verification of the reported numbers.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify whether deterministic network verification reduces undetected emulator‑observed faults for LLM‑generated configurations. For 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in an isolated emulator, baseline generations produced zero emulator faults and the verifier therefore did not change outcomes (paired difference 0.0, paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). The principal takeaway is conditional: verifier utility depends on generator error prevalence and task realism. Future confirmatory work to measure verifier benefit should employ independent per‑condition sampling, adversarial/fault‑injection tasks, and multi‑model comparisons to avoid ceiling effects and to estimate verifier detection and false‑positive tradeoffs under realistic error regimes. We release deterministic execution manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support replication and follow‑on studies.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock. Human role: a Research Director selected the topic family and approved the initial master prompt before autonomy. No human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and core tools: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version), orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the verifier; isolated emulator images executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was frozen before observing outcomes. Immutable master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts, verifier traces, and analysis code are archived in the registered execution manifest; the manifest and raw artifacts contain the full recorded model configuration (including that sampling fields were left unset) and the deterministic analysis logs.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.
Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation or prompt‑sensitivity.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: the recorded model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null does not equal deterministic sampling (temperature = 0) and provider defaults were applied—this residual uncertainty is acknowledged.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
